newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK -- More selling seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK -- More selling seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are expected to continue giving up ground Thursday, as the market nervously awaits Friday's employment report, traders and analysts said.
But the magnitude of the declines shouldn't be all that significant, players said.

"We'll correct a little more," said a trader at a primary dealership, noting that Treasuries fell about a quarter-point on Thursday, after surging two points Wednesday. "We'll go into the (employment) number bearish and sell off into Friday."

Late Wednesday, the 30-year Treasury bond was at 100-19/32, down 8/32 from Tuesday. Its yield ticked up one basis point to 6.70 percent. The two-year note was down 2/32 to 100-5/32 to yield 5.79 percent.
"Considering $100 billion (in new supply) was announced, the market held in," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.
Although the market is awaiting Friday's October employment numbers, players are also jittery over the upcoming bills and note auctions next week.
But before the market gets caught up in supply, it must first deal with the next couple days of economic news.
Thursday, the key report is the Chicago Purchasing Managers' survey for October, due at 1000 EST/1400 GMT. After September's 56.3 reading, the market anticipates a slight decline.
Merrill's Dennis said that for the market to react favorably, it needs to come in at around 50. She noted that vendor deliveries, employment and price components will also be carefully watched.
Also scheduled for release Thursday are personal income and spending data for September, as well as jobless claims for the week ended Oct. 26 -- both due at 0830 EST/1230 GMT.
Neither release is expected to have much market impact, analysts said. Plus, they said, it's unlikely Treasuries will break out of recent ranges.
"It's time to wait and see what nonfarm payrolls have to offer," said Jerry Zukowski, a fixed income economist at PaineWebber Inc. "I would be surprised at if it did much before employment."
Federal Funds are expected to open at 5-3/8 percent to 5-1/2 percent -- above the 5-1/4 percent target rate.
